title: Derived units in base-unit form

learning_outcomes.text: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

prior_knowledge_summary: Mass, length, time, electric current and temperature use the SI base units kg, m, s, A and K.
A prefix can be replaced by its fixed power-of-ten multiplier, with units kept attached throughout a conversion.
new_learning: A derived unit is built by multiplying or dividing SI base units.
A named derived unit can be replaced by base units before powers are collected and cancelled.
A supplied relationship can be rearranged and used as a route to the base units of an unfamiliar quantity or constant.
not_yet_taught: Checking whether the units on both sides of an equation are homogeneous.
Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

visual_planning.reason: Six distinct visuals establish the opening identity puzzle, show how derived units are built, model cancellation and negative powers, demonstrate two complete unit routes, and expose a common reversal error.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Can two different-looking labels mean the same unit?
content: One energy meter is labelled J. Another is labelled kg m^2 s^-2. A student says the meters cannot measure the same quantity because the labels are different. Is that conclusion safe?
A named unit can be a short label for a combination of base units. Today we will unpack those labels and build unfamiliar units from supplied relationships.

figure.purpose: Create a unit-identity puzzle that makes base-unit expansion necessary
figure.brief: Draw two simple hand-sketched meter cards on white paper. One card is labelled J and the other kg m^2 s^-2. Put a question mark between them and the note same quantity? Do not reveal the answer.
figure.alt_text: Two meter cards are labelled joule and kilogram metre squared per second squared, with a question asking whether they represent the same unit.

blocks.title: Derived units are built from base units
content: The five base units from the previous lesson are our building pieces: kg, m, s, A and K. A derived quantity combines base quantities, so its unit combines their base units.
Area is length multiplied by length, so its unit is m x m = m^2. Volume is length multiplied three times, so its unit is m^3. Speed is distance divided by time, so its unit is m/s, written m s^-1.
A negative power means division. The form s^-1 means one divided by s, and m^-3 means one divided by m^3. This compact form makes long products and quotients easier to simplify.

figure.purpose: Connect familiar geometric and rate quantities to products and quotients of base units
figure.brief: Create a three-panel teacher sketch. Show a square with m by m leading to m^2, a cube with three metre edges leading to m^3, and a short route over a stopwatch leading to m/s then m s^-1. Use a different colour for multiplication and division.
figure.alt_text: Three panels build square metres, cubic metres and metres per second from metre and second base units.

blocks.title: Unpack force, then build energy and power
content: Use the supplied relationship force = mass x acceleration. Acceleration has unit m s^-2, so force has unit kg x m s^-2 = kg m s^-2. The named unit newton, N, is shorthand for this base-unit product.
For this unit exercise, use the supplied relationship energy transferred = force x distance. Replace N before simplifying: J = N m = (kg m s^-2)m = kg m^2 s^-2.
Power is energy transferred divided by time. Therefore W = J/s = (kg m^2 s^-2)/s = kg m^2 s^-3. Each step begins with a relationship, replaces named units, and then collects powers.

figure.purpose: Show a complete chain from base units to force, energy and power
figure.brief: Draw a vertical unit-building flow on white paper: kg and m s^-2 combine to N, N and m combine to J, then J divided by s gives W. Beside each named unit, show its fully expanded base-unit form. Keep arrows clear and annotations short.
figure.alt_text: A vertical flow expands newton, joule and watt into SI base-unit combinations.

blocks.title: Rearrange first when the required unit is hidden
content: Suppose a supplied model is F = krv, where F is force, r is radius, v is speed and k is a constant. We are not learning the motion in this context. We only use the supplied relationship as a unit route.
Rearrange to k = F/(rv). Now substitute units: [k] = (kg m s^-2)/[m(m s^-1)]. The denominator is m^2 s^-1.

Subtract the denominator powers from the numerator powers. This gives kg m^(1-2) s^(-2-(-1)) = kg m^-1 s^-1. Check the cancellation visually: one of the two denominator metres cancels the numerator metre, leaving m^-1.

figure.purpose: Model rearrangement, substitution and cancellation for an unfamiliar constant
figure.brief: Create an annotated four-line notebook layout for F = krv, k = F/(rv), base-unit substitution, and kg m^-1 s^-1. Use strike-through cancellation marks on one metre and colour the time powers that combine. Do not include any numerical values.
figure.alt_text: A four-line unit derivation rearranges a supplied force model and simplifies the constant to kilogram per metre per second.

blocks.title: Electric charge brings current and time together
content: Some relationships need a short bridge before all units are in base form. Use the supplied relationship charge = current x time, so charge has base unit A s.
For the supplied model v = mu F/e, rearrange to mu = ve/F. Speed has unit m s^-1, charge has unit A s, and force has unit kg m s^-2.
Substitute and simplify: [mu] = (m s^-1)(A s)/(kg m s^-2) = A kg^-1 s^2. The metre cancels, and s^-1 x s gives no time factor in the numerator before division by s^-2 produces s^2.
An independent check is to write the quotient as multiplication by the reciprocal: (m s^-1)(A s)(kg^-1 m^-1 s^2). The same cancellations give A kg^-1 s^2.

figure.purpose: Teach the A s bridge for charge and verify a complex unit by a second representation
figure.brief: Draw two parallel routes on a white-paper sketch. The first uses a fraction for (m s^-1)(A s)/(kg m s^-2). The second multiplies by the reciprocal. Use matching colours to show identical metre and time cancellations, ending at A kg^-1 s^2.
figure.alt_text: Two equivalent unit-cancellation routes use charge as ampere seconds and both produce ampere second squared per kilogram.

blocks.title: Dividing by a unit reverses its powers
content: It can feel natural to copy every power unchanged from a denominator because the symbols are still visible. That loses the meaning of division.
For example, density is mass divided by volume. Its unit is kg/m^3 = kg m^-3, not kg m^3. The negative power records that volume is in the denominator.
Use one of two safe routes: keep a fraction until cancellation is finished, or change every denominator power when you write its reciprocal. Do not mix the routes halfway through.

figure.purpose: Contrast the correct reciprocal power with a plausible denominator-copying error
figure.brief: Draw a balance-style comparison. On the left, show kg/m^3 leading to kg m^-3 with a green reciprocal arrow. On the right, show the common error kg m^3 with a small correction mark and the note denominator means negative power. Keep the correct route visually dominant.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows that kilograms divided by cubic metres is kilogram metre to the minus three, not kilogram metre cubed.

blocks.title: A reliable four-step unit route
content: First write or rearrange the supplied relationship for the required quantity. Second replace every named or derived unit with SI base units.

Third keep products and quotients visible while you collect powers and cancel matching factors. Fourth rewrite the result using positive or negative powers and check it with a fraction or reciprocal form.

The opening labels can describe the same energy unit because J = kg m^2 s^-2. We have only expressed units in base-unit form. We have not compared the two sides of a candidate equation. Equation homogeneity belongs to the next lesson.

concepts_taught: derived units are products or quotients of SI base units
named derived units can be expanded before powers are simplified
supplied relationships can be rearranged to derive the base units of an unfamiliar quantity or constant
representations_used: area, volume and speed comparison panels
misconceptions_addressed: different-looking unit labels must represent different quantities
negative powers can be copied from denominators without reversing sign
named units can be left unexpanded during a base-unit derivation
skills_students_can_now_use: express common derived units as products or quotients of SI base units
replace N, J and W with base-unit forms when supplied relationships support the route
use A s as the base-unit form of charge when a supplied relationship requires it
rearrange a supplied relationship and simplify the units of an unfamiliar constant
check a unit simplification using an equivalent fraction or reciprocal form
next_lesson_can_assume: the base-unit forms kg m s^-2 for force, kg m^2 s^-2 for energy and kg m^2 s^-3 for power
derived-unit products and quotients can be simplified by collecting powers
the base units of an unfamiliar quantity can be derived from a supplied relationship

that matching units prove an equation is physically correct
